subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 13! In this unit you will learn how mathematicians compare quantities and how they scale things up and down while keeping them in exactly the same relationship. This is the world of ratio and proportion, and once you can see it, you will notice it everywhere. When Amina makes a necklace at the Hargeisa market with blue and white beads, when Hassan mixes paint for a wall, when Khadija doubles a bariis recipe to feed extra guests at a family dinner, or when a mapmaker shrinks the whole distance from Mogadishu to Kismaayo onto a single page, they are all using ratio and proportion.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Mathematics 0096 — Stage 5 workbook source documents for screen presentation.

outcomes: Write a ratio using the colon notation (for example 3:2) and read it correctly.
Describe a ratio with ‘for every’ language and a proportion with ‘out of’ language.
Simplify a ratio to its lowest terms by dividing by the highest common factor.
Recognise and generate equivalent ratios using ratio tables.
Share a total quantity in a given ratio, including three-part ratios.
Solve direct proportion problems using the unit (one-part) method.
Use ratio and proportion to scale recipes, maps and models up or down.
Tell the difference between a ratio (part to part) and a proportion (part to whole), and convert proportions to fractions, decimals and percentages.

concepts.title: What a Ratio Is and How We Write It
concepts.explanation:
A ratio compares two or more quantities by showing how many of one thing there are for each amount of another. A good way to hear a ratio is to ask: “For every ___ of this, how many of that do we have?” Ratios are all about the phrase ‘for every’.

Let us start with a real example. Amina is threading a necklace to sell at the market. She uses 6 blue beads and 2 white beads. The ratio of blue beads to white beads is written 6:2, using the colon symbol, and we read it aloud as “six to two.” The colon is like the word ‘to’. So 3:1 means “three to one,” 2:5 means “two to five,” and a three-part ratio like 4:3:2 means “four to three to two.”

There are two ideas about ratios you must never forget. First, order matters. The ratio 3:1 is not the same as 1:3. If we say the ratio of blue beads to white beads is 3:1, that means there are more blue beads. If we wrote 1:3 instead, we would be saying there are more white beads – a completely different necklace. Always write the terms in the order named. Second, a ratio compares part to part. In Amina’s necklace we are comparing blue beads with white beads, not blue beads with the total number of beads. Comparing a part with the whole is a different idea called proportion, which we will meet soon.
concepts.example: Ratios appear far beyond bead-work. On a football pitch the ratio of players to referees might be 22:1. In Hassan’s family the ratio of goats to camels might be 8:3. In a class at Nuur Academy the ratio of boys to girls might be 3:2. Each time, the ratio captures a comparison in a short, tidy form. Learning to write these comparisons quickly and correctly is your first skill in this unit.

concepts.title: Simplifying Ratios to Lowest Terms
concepts.explanation:
Ratios behave much like fractions. Just as the fraction 6/8 can be written more simply as 3/4, the ratio 6:2 can be written more simply as 3:1. Simplifying a ratio means dividing every term by the same number until you cannot divide any further. The result is called the ratio in its lowest terms.

Look again at Amina’s necklace: the ratio of blue to white beads is 6:2. Both terms can be divided by 2. Doing so gives 6 ÷ 2 = 3 and 2 ÷ 2 = 1, so 6:2 = 3:1. This tells us something beautifully simple: “for every 3 blue beads, there is 1 white bead.” The simplified ratio is easier to picture and easier to use.

To simplify quickly, look for the highest common factor of the terms – the largest number that divides them all exactly. Consider the ratio 12:8. The number 4 divides both 12 and 8, and it is the largest number that does so, so 4 is the highest common factor. Dividing gives 12 ÷ 4 = 3 and 8 ÷ 4 = 2, so 12:8 = 3:2. If you cannot spot the highest common factor at once, you may divide in smaller steps: 12:8 halves to 6:4, which halves again to 3:2. You reach the same lowest terms either way.

Here are three more to study carefully. The ratio 18:12 shares a common factor of 6, so 18:12 = 3:2. The ratio 20:35 shares a common factor of 5, so 20:35 = 4:7. The ratio 24:16 shares a common factor of 8, so 24:16 = 3:2. Notice that a ratio is fully simplified only when the terms have no common factor left except 1. In 3:2, nothing except 1 divides both 3 and 2, so 3:2 is truly in lowest terms.
concepts.example: Simplifying also works for three-part ratios. In a paint mix of Red:Blue:Green = 4:6:2, every term can be divided by 2, giving 2:3:1. Whenever you finish a ratio question, it is good manners in mathematics to leave your answer in its simplest form, just as you would tidy your work before showing it to your teacher.

concepts.title: Equivalent Ratios and Ratio Tables
concepts.explanation:
Equivalent ratios are different-looking ratios that describe exactly the same relationship, in the same way that 1/2, 2/4 and 3/6 are equivalent fractions. For example, 2:3, 4:6, 6:9 and 8:12 are all equivalent. Each one says “for every 2 of the first thing there are 3 of the second thing” – they are just written at different sizes.

To make an equivalent ratio, you multiply or divide both terms by the same number. Starting with 2:3 and multiplying both terms by 2 gives 4:6. Multiplying both terms by 3 gives 6:9. Multiplying both terms by 4 gives 8:12. Going the other way, if you were given 8:12 you could divide both terms by 4 to simplify back to 2:3. The relationship never changes as long as you treat both terms in exactly the same way.

Here is the single most important warning in this whole unit: you must do the same operation to both terms. A common mistake is to add the same number to each term – that does not keep a ratio equivalent. For instance, 2:3 is not equivalent to 3:4, even though we added 1 to each term, because 2:3 means the first is smaller by one part in three, while 3:4 means something different. To keep a ratio the same, you must multiply or divide, never add or subtract.

A ratio table is a neat tool for showing equivalent ratios and spotting the pattern. Imagine mixing orange paint with red and yellow in the ratio 3:2. We can build a table where every column keeps the same relationship:
concepts.example: Reading across the table, the red row counts up in threes and the yellow row counts up in twos, but every column shows the same 3:2 relationship. Ratio tables help you find a missing amount quickly: if you know you have 12 cups of red paint, run your finger down that column to read off 8 cups of yellow. Zahra keeps a small ratio table in her notebook whenever she mixes colours, so the shade never changes.

concepts.title: Sharing a Quantity in a Ratio
concepts.explanation:
One of the most useful things a ratio can do is help you share a total fairly. Suppose Omar and Yusuf sell mangoes together at the market and agree to split the money in the ratio 3:2, because Omar did more of the work. At the end of the day they have earned 60 shillings. How much should each boy receive? This is a sharing in a ratio problem, and there is a reliable four-step method.

Add the parts of the ratio to find the total number of parts. For 3:2, the total is 3 + 2 = 5 parts.

Divide the total quantity by the number of parts to find the value of one part. Here, 60 ÷ 5 = 12 shillings per part.

Multiply each share by the value of one part. Omar gets 3 × 12 = 36 shillings; Yusuf gets 2 × 12 = 24 shillings.

Check by adding the shares back together. 36 + 24 = 60 shillings, which matches the total, so the answer is correct.

The heart of this method is the idea of one part. A ratio breaks the whole into equal parts, and once you know what a single part is worth, you can build any share you like. In Omar and Yusuf’s case, each part was worth 12 shillings, and their shares were simply 3 parts and 2 parts of that same size.

This method works just as well for three-part ratios. A painter mixes red, blue and yellow paint in the ratio 1:2:3 to make 12 litres of a special colour. First add the parts: 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 parts. Next find one part: 12 ÷ 6 = 2 litres per part. Finally multiply: red is 1 × 2 = 2 litres, blue is 2 × 2 = 4 litres, and yellow is 3 × 2 = 6 litres. Check: 2 + 4 + 6 = 12 litres. The same four steps carry you safely through, no matter how many parts the ratio has.
concepts.example: Sharing in a ratio comes up constantly in real life. When a grandmother divides a plate of dates between two grandchildren by age, when Hani and Sagal split the cost of a football, or when land is shared between family members, the fair answer is found by turning the sharing into parts, working out the value of one part, and then building each share. Whenever you feel unsure, whisper to yourself: “Add the parts, find one part, then multiply.”

concepts.title: Direct Proportion and the Unit Method
concepts.explanation:
Two quantities are in direct proportion when they grow and shrink together at the same rate. If you double one, the other doubles too. If you halve one, the other halves. Direct proportion is the mathematics behind recipes, shopping, and fair pricing, and the most powerful tool for solving it is the unit method – find the value of one, then multiply.

Here is a shopping example. In the market, 3 pencils cost 6 shillings. How much do 9 pencils cost? Using the unit method, first find the cost of one pencil: 6 ÷ 3 = 2 shillings each. Then multiply by the number you want: 9 × 2 = 18 shillings. The two quantities – number of pencils and total cost – stayed in direct proportion the whole time, because three times as many pencils cost three times as much.

Cooking is full of direct proportion. Khadija has a rice dish that serves 4 people and uses 2 cups of rice and 3 cups of water. She needs to serve 12 people at a family gathering. Because 12 ÷ 4 = 3, she is making three times as much, so she multiplies every ingredient by 3: rice becomes 2 × 3 = 6 cups, and water becomes 3 × 3 = 9 cups. Notice that the ratio of rice to water stays exactly 2:3 – that is what keeps the dish tasting right. Scaling a recipe is really just keeping quantities in direct proportion.

Sometimes the numbers do not divide so neatly, and that is exactly when the unit method saves you. Suppose a pancake recipe serves 4 people using 2 cups of flour, and you must serve 10 people. Find one serving first: 2 ÷ 4 = 0.5 cups of flour per person. Then multiply by 10: 0.5 × 10 = 5 cups of flour. Because you found the amount for one person, you can build the amount for any number of people. The unit method is a key that unlocks every direct proportion problem, tidy or untidy.
concepts.example: Direct proportion also lets you compare value when shopping, which is a real skill for saving money. Suppose Brand A sells 500 g of dates for 4 shillings and Brand B sells 750 g for 6 shillings. To compare fairly, find the price of the same amount – say one gram, or better, one kilogram. Brand A works out to 8 shillings per kilogram, and Brand B works out to 8 shillings per kilogram too, so in this case they are equal value. Finding a common unit is how you decide which shop truly offers the better deal.

concepts.title: Scaling with Maps and Models
concepts.explanation:
A scale is a special ratio that compares the size of a drawing or model with the size of the real thing. Scales let a whole city fit on a page and let an architect hold a building in the palm of a hand. A scale is usually written as a ratio such as 1:100, which means “1 unit on the model stands for 100 of the same units in real life.”

Think about a model of a building where the scale is 1:100. This tells us that 1 cm on the model represents 100 cm – that is 1 metre – in reality. So a door that measures 3 cm on the model stands for a real door 3 metres tall, because 3 × 100 = 300 cm = 3 m. To go from model to real life you multiply by the scale; to go from real life to model you divide by the scale.

Maps use scale in exactly the same way. Suppose a map has a scale of 1:25,000, and two schools are 6 cm apart on the map. To find the real distance, multiply: 6 × 25,000 = 150,000 cm. Now convert to a friendlier unit: 150,000 cm = 1,500 m = 1.5 km. So the two schools are 1.5 km apart in real life. The scale did all the heavy lifting; your job was to multiply and then convert the units carefully. Ibrahim uses map scales like this to work out how far it is to walk between towns.
concepts.example: Scaling also explains how photographs are enlarged without looking stretched or squashed. If a photo is enlarged so that 3 cm becomes 8 cm, the scale factor is 8 ÷ 3. A width of 12 cm in the original then becomes 12 × 8 ÷ 3 = 32 cm in the enlargement. As long as every length is multiplied by the same scale factor, the picture keeps its correct shape. This is why a model aeroplane looks exactly like a real aeroplane: every part has been shrunk by the very same ratio.

methods.title: How to simplify a ratio
methods.example: In a class of 24 students there are 15 girls and 9 boys. Write the ratio of girls to boys in its simplest form.
steps: Find the highest common factor of the terms.
Divide every term by that factor.
Check that no number except 1 divides all the terms.

methods.title: How to share a quantity in a ratio
methods.example: The ratio of cats to dogs in a shelter is 4:7. If there are 16 cats, how many dogs are there?
steps: Add the parts of the ratio to find the total number of parts.
Divide the total quantity by the number of parts to find one part.
Multiply each share by the value of one part.
Check by adding all the shares back to the original total.

methods.title: How to solve a direct proportion (unit method)
methods.example: Two numbers are in the ratio 2:5. If their sum is 35, what are the two numbers?
steps: Find the value of one item by dividing.
Multiply by how many items you want.
Check the two quantities grew at the same rate.

methods.title: How to use a map or model scale
methods.example: A recipe uses flour and sugar in the ratio 3:2. If you use 9 cups of flour, how much sugar do you need?
steps: Model to real life: multiply by the scale.
Real life to model: divide by the scale.
Convert units carefully: 100 cm = 1 m, 1,000 m = 1 km.

methods.title: Use the unit method
methods.example: If 3 pencils cost 2 shillings, how much do 12 pencils cost?
steps: Find the cost of one pencil first: 2 ÷ 3 shillings each.
Then multiply by 12: (2 ÷ 3) × 12 = 2 × 12 ÷ 3 = 24 ÷ 3 = 8 shillings.
The unit method handled the tricky division for us.

methods.title: Turn a proportion into a percentage
methods.example: Express 7 out of 20 as a percentage.
steps: The proportion is the fraction 7/20.
Divide to make a decimal: 7 ÷ 20 = 0.35.
Multiply by 100 to make a percentage: 0.35 × 100 = 35%.
So 7 out of 20 is the same as 35%.

workedExamples.title: Write and simplify a ratio
workedExamples.prompt: In a class of 24 students there are 15 girls and 9 boys. Write the ratio of girls to boys in its simplest form.
workedExamples.solution: The ratio of girls to boys is 15:9. The highest common factor of 15 and 9 is 3. Dividing both terms by 3 gives 15 ÷ 3 = 5 and 9 ÷ 3 = 3, so the simplest form is 5:3. This means for every 5 girls there are 3 boys.

workedExamples.title: Find a missing value in a ratio
workedExamples.prompt: The ratio of cats to dogs in a shelter is 4:7. If there are 16 cats, how many dogs are there?
workedExamples.solution: The number of cats went from 4 up to 16, which is ×4 (because 16 ÷ 4 = 4). To keep the ratio equivalent, multiply the dogs by the same 4: 7 × 4 = 28 dogs. Check: 16:28 simplifies by dividing by 4 back to 4:7, which matches.

workedExamples.title: Share a quantity in a ratio
workedExamples.prompt: Two numbers are in the ratio 2:5. If their sum is 35, what are the two numbers?
workedExamples.solution: Add the parts: 2 + 5 = 7 parts. Find one part: 35 ÷ 7 = 5. Multiply: the first number is 2 × 5 = 10, and the second is 5 × 5 = 25. Check: 10 + 25 = 35, and 10:25 simplifies to 2:5. Correct.

workedExamples.title: Scale a recipe (direct proportion)
workedExamples.prompt: A recipe uses flour and sugar in the ratio 3:2. If you use 9 cups of flour, how much sugar do you need?
workedExamples.solution: The flour went from 3 up to 9, which is ×3. Keep the ratio by multiplying the sugar by 3 as well: 2 × 3 = 6 cups of sugar. The ratio stays 9:6, which simplifies back to 3:2.

workedExamples.title: Use the unit method
workedExamples.prompt: If 3 pencils cost 2 shillings, how much do 12 pencils cost?
workedExamples.solution: Find the cost of one pencil first: 2 ÷ 3 shillings each. Then multiply by 12: (2 ÷ 3) × 12 = 2 × 12 ÷ 3 = 24 ÷ 3 = 8 shillings. The unit method handled the tricky division for us.

workedExamples.title: Turn a proportion into a percentage
workedExamples.prompt: Express 7 out of 20 as a percentage.
workedExamples.solution: The proportion is the fraction 7/20. Divide to make a decimal: 7 ÷ 20 = 0.35. Multiply by 100 to make a percentage: 0.35 × 100 = 35%. So 7 out of 20 is the same as 35%.

workedExamples.title: A map-scale problem
workedExamples.prompt: On a map with scale 1:25,000, two towns are 6 cm apart. What is the real distance in kilometres?
workedExamples.solution: Multiply the map distance by the scale: 6 × 25,000 = 150,000 cm. Convert: 150,000 cm = 1,500 m = 1.5 km. Remember to keep dividing by 100 for metres and by 1,000 for kilometres.

workedExamples.title: Share a three-part ratio
workedExamples.prompt: Three numbers are in the ratio 2:3:5 and their sum is 60. Find all three numbers.
workedExamples.solution: Add the parts: 2 + 3 + 5 = 10 parts. Find one part: 60 ÷ 10 = 6. Multiply each: 2 × 6 = 12, 3 × 6 = 18, 5 × 6 = 30. Check: 12 + 18 + 30 = 60. Correct.

workedExamples.title: Express each proportion as a percentage
workedExamples.prompt: Express each proportion as a percentage: a) 3 out of 10 b) 7 out of 20 c) 9 out of 25.

workedExamples.title: If 3 pencils cost 2 shillings, how much do 12 pencils…
workedExamples.prompt: If 3 pencils cost 2 shillings, how much do 12 pencils cost? Use the unit method.
workedExamples.solution: Find the cost of one pencil first: 2 ÷ 3 shillings each. Then multiply by 12: (2 ÷ 3) × 12 = 24 ÷ 3 = 8 shillings.

workedExamples.title: A paint mix uses red and yellow in the ratio 2:5. If…
workedExamples.prompt: A paint mix uses red and yellow in the ratio 2:5. If you use 6 litres of red, how much yellow do you need?
workedExamples.solution: The red went from 2 up to 6, which is ×3. Keep the ratio by multiplying the yellow by 3 too: 5 × 3 = 15 litres of yellow.

workedExamples.title: Three numbers are in the ratio 2:3:5 and their sum is…
workedExamples.prompt: Three numbers are in the ratio 2:3:5 and their sum is 60. Find all three numbers.
workedExamples.solution: Add the parts: 2 + 3 + 5 = 10 parts. Find one part: 60 ÷ 10 = 6. Multiply each: 2 × 6 = 12, 3 × 6 = 18, 5 × 6 = 30. Check: 12 + 18 + 30 = 60.

activities.title: Recipe Master Chef
activities.materials: paper, a pencil, measuring cups (optional), and a simple recipe.
steps: Take Khadija’s rice recipe that serves 4 people: 2 cups of rice and 3 cups of water.
Scale it to serve 8 people by multiplying every ingredient by 2. Write down the new amounts.
Now scale it to serve 12 people. What did you multiply by this time?
Scale it back down to serve just 2 people. What is the ratio of rice to water each time?
You should find the ratio of rice to water stays 2:3 no matter how many people you serve. That constant ratio is what keeps the dish tasting right.

activities.title: Bead Necklace Ratios
activities.materials: beads, buttons, or small stones in two colours, and some string.
steps: Make a pattern with blue and white beads in the ratio 3:1 (three blue, then one white, repeating).
After making the pattern five times, count your beads. What is the ratio now? Simplify it.
Work out the proportion of beads that are blue as a fraction and a percentage.
Try a new ratio, such as 2:3, and describe your necklace using ‘for every’ language.

activities.title: Fair Share Investigation
activities.materials: counters, dried beans, or small stones to act as ‘shillings’.
steps: Count out 40 ‘shillings’. Share them between two people in the ratio 3:5 using the four-step method.
Check your shares add back to 40. Did each person get a whole number of shillings?
Now share 24 dates between three cousins in the ratio 3:2:1. How many parts are there in total?
Invent your own sharing problem for a family member or your AI tutor, and let them solve it.

activities.title: Map and Scale Adventure
activities.materials: a ruler, paper, and a printed or drawn map with a scale.
steps: Draw a simple map of your neighbourhood where 1 cm stands for 100 m (a scale of 1:10,000).
Mark your home, the library, and the market. Measure the distances in centimetres.
Multiply each distance by the scale to find the real distance in metres, then in kilometres.
Challenge: if you walk at about 5 km per hour, how long would each journey take?

activities.title: Paint and Colour Mixing (Maths Game)
activities.materials: two players (or you and your AI tutor), and coloured counters or pencils.
steps: Player 1 names a colour ratio, such as red to yellow = 2:5.
Player 2 must lay out counters to match, then simplify or scale the ratio on request.
Score a point for each correct ratio and each correct simplification.
Swap roles and play to ten points. Keep a ratio table to check each other’s work.

activities.title: Shopping Value Detective (Family Task)
activities.materials: two similar products with different sizes and prices (or make some up).
steps: Find two packets of the same food in different sizes, for example 500 g for 4 shillings and 750 g for 6 shillings.
Work out the price of the same amount for each, such as the price per 100 g or per kilogram.
Decide which packet gives better value for money, and explain your reasoning to your family.
Do this for three more pairs of products and record which was better value each time.

After your activities, talk or write about: Which activity helped you understand ratio and proportion best? What was the trickiest part? Where in your daily life do you now notice ratios – in cooking, shopping, sharing, or maps? Share your answers with your teacher at your next session.

rules.title: Ratio Rule
rules.text: A ratio compares part to part, written with a colon: 3:2 is read three to two. Order matters: 3:2 is not the same as 2:3. Simplify by dividing every term by the same number.

rules.title: Equivalent Ratio Rule
rules.text: Multiply or divide both terms by the same number to keep a ratio equivalent. Never add or subtract: 2:3 is not equivalent to 3:4.

rules.title: Proportion Rule
rules.text: A proportion compares a part to the whole. It can be written as a fraction, a decimal, or a percentage. 6 out of 8 = 6/8 = 3/4 = 0.75 = 75%.

reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Length 18 m, width 12 m (60 ÷ 2 = 30 m for length + width; 3 + 2 = 5 parts, 30 ÷ 5 = 6, so length = 3 × 6 = 18 m and width = 2 × 6 = 12 m).

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Two solutions are mixed in the ratio 3:2. Solution A is 20% salt and Solution B is 35% salt. Find the salt percentage of the mixture.
Explain the key idea in Scaling with Maps and Models.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer:
A scale is a special ratio that compares the size of a drawing or model with the size of the real thing. Scales let a whole city fit on a page and let an architect hold a building in the palm of a hand. A scale is usually written as a ratio such as 1:100, which means “1 unit on the model stands for 100 of the same units in real life.”

Think about a model of a building where the scale is 1:100. This tells us that 1 cm on the model represents 100 cm – that is 1 metre – in reality. So a door that measures 3 cm on the model stands for a real door 3 metres tall, because 3 × 100 = 300 cm = 3 m. To go from model to real life you multiply by the scale; to go from real life to model you divide by the scale.

rounds.prompt: In a classroom there are 18 boys and 12 girls. What is the ratio of boys to girls in its simplest form?
rounds.clue: Find the highest common factor of both terms first.
rounds.explanation: 18:12 simplifies by dividing both terms by 6, giving 3:2.

selfAssessment: I can write a ratio using the colon notation (for example 3:2) and read it correctly.
I can describe a ratio with ‘for every’ language and a proportion with ‘out of’ language.
I can simplify a ratio to its lowest terms by dividing by the highest common factor.
I can recognise and generate equivalent ratios using ratio tables.
I can share a total quantity in a given ratio, including three-part ratios.
I can solve direct proportion problems using the unit (one-part) method.
I can use ratio and proportion to scale recipes, maps and models up or down.
I can tell the difference between a ratio (part to part) and a proportion (part to whole), and convert proportions to fractions, decimals and percentages.
